title: History of the automobile
wiki_lead:
Crude ideas and designs of automobiles can be traced back to ancient and medieval times. In 1649, Hans Hautsch of Nuremberg built a clockwork-driven carriage. In 1672, a small-scale steam-powered vehicle was created by Ferdinand Verbiest; the first steam-powered automobile capable of human transportation was built by Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot in 1769. Inventors began to branch out at the start of the 19th century, creating the de Rivaz engine, one of the first internal combustion engines, and an early electric motor. Samuel Brown later tested the first industrially applied internal combustion engine in 1826. Only two of these were made.
Development was hindered in the mid-19th century by a backlash against large vehicles, yet progress continued on some internal combustion engines. The engine evolved as engineers created two- and four-cycle combustion engines and began using gasoline. The first modern car—a practical, marketable automobile for everyday use—and the first car in series production appeared in 1886, when Carl Benz developed a gasoline-powered automobile and made several identical copies. In 1890, Gottlieb Daimler, inventor of the high-speed liquid petroleum-fueled engine, and Wilhelm Maybach formed Daimler Motoren Gesellschaft. In 1926, the company merged with Benz & Cie. (founded by Carl Benz in 1883) to form Daimler-Benz, known for its Mercedes-Benz automobile brand.
From 1886, many inventors and entrepreneurs got into the "horseless carriage" business, both in America and Europe, and inventions and innovations rapidly furthered the development and production of automobiles. Ransom E. Olds founded Oldsmobile in 1897, and introduced the Curved Dash Oldsmobile in 1901. Olds pioneered the assembly line using identical, interchangeable parts, producing thousands of Oldsmobiles by 1903. Although sources differ, approximately 19,000 Oldsmobiles were built, with the last produced in 1907. Production likely peaked from 1903 through 1905, at up to 5,000 units a year. In 1908, the Ford Motor Company further revolutionized automobile production by developing and selling its Ford Model T at a relatively modest price. From 1913, introducing an advanced moving assembly line allowed Ford to lower the Model T's price by almost 50%, making it the first mass-affordable automobile.

Power sources
The early automobile history concentrated on searching for a reliable portable power unit to propel the vehicle.


Steam-powered wheeled vehicles


17th and 18th centuries

Ferdinand Verbiest, a member of a Jesuit mission in China, built a steam-powered vehicle around 1672 as a toy for the Kangxi Emperor. It was small-scale and could not carry a driver, but it was, perhaps, the first working steam-powered vehicle ('auto-mobile').
Steam-powered self-propelled vehicles large enough to transport people and cargo were devised in the late 18th century. Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot demonstrated his fardier à vapeur ("steam dray"), an experimental steam-driven artillery tract
grok_lead: The history of the automobile spans the invention and evolution of self-propelled road vehicles, from rudimentary steam-powered prototypes in the late 18th century to the mass-produced internal combustion engine cars that reshaped global society in the 20th century. No single individual invented the automobile, but early concepts trace back to designs by Leonardo da Vinci in the 15th century, with practical developments emerging through contributions from multiple engineers across Europe. In 1769, French military engineer Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot built the first self-propelled vehicle, a steam-powered fardier Ã  vapeur capable of carrying artillery, marking the initial step toward mechanized transport. The transition to more viable designs accelerated in the 19th century with experiments in steam, electric, and gasoline power. Scottish inventor Robert Anderson constructed one of the first electric carriages between 1832 and 1839, though it was limited by short battery life and slow speeds. By the 1880s, German engineers Karl Benz and Gottlieb Daimler independently advanced internal combustion technology; Benz patented his three-wheeled Benz Patent-Motorwagen on January 29, 1886 (DRP No. 37435), widely regarded as the first practical automobile due to its integrated design combining the engine, chassis, steering, and brakes. The designation of the "first automobile" remains debated among historians depending on criteria such as propulsion type and practical utility, with some authoritative sources crediting Cugnot's 1769 steam vehicle as the first true self-propelled road vehicle while others highlight Benz's contributions to the modern gasoline-powered era. while Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach developed a four-wheeled motorized carriage with a high-speed gasoline engine the same year. The practicality of Benz's vehicle was demonstrated by Bertha Benz's pioneering long-distance drive of over 100 km from Mannheim to Pforzheim in August 1888. These innovations laid the foundation for the industry, with Benz's vehicle achieving speeds up to 10 miles per hour and featuring key components like a horizontal single-cylinder engine. The early 20th century marked the automobile's commercialization and societal integration, driven by American industrialists. Henry Ford founded the Ford Motor Company in 1903 and launched the Model T in 1908 at $825, an affordable design that sold over 15 million units by 1927 through innovations like interchangeable parts and vanadium steel for durability. Ford's introduction of the moving assembly line at his Highland Park plant in 1913-1914 drastically reduced production timeâfrom 12 hours to about 90 minutes per vehicleâlowering costs to as little as $290 by the 1920s and making cars accessible to the middle class. This mass production era spurred the growth of companies like General Motors, founded by William Durant in 1908, and Oldsmobile, which produced over 5,000 vehicles in 1904 under Ransom E. Olds. By 1910, U.S. automobile output had surpassed horse-drawn wagons, with sales climbing from 181,000 units in 1910 to 4.5 million by 1929, creating jobs in manufacturing, dealerships, and related services. The interwar and post-World War II periods saw the automobile's global expansion and profound economic impacts. In rural America, the Model T facilitated farm mechanization and reduced isolation, with one in three farmers owning a car by 1920; it also boosted road infrastructure, as states like Virginia increased surfaced roads from 7% in 1914 to 21% by 1930. World War II shifted production to military vehicles, but postwar demand fueled rapid growth, particularly in Europe and Japan, where companies like Toyota emerged as leaders by the 1980s. Safety features evolved gradually, with seat belts becoming standard in the 1960s and airbags in the 1970s, addressing rising accident rates amid booming car ownership. In the late 20th and early 21st centuries, environmental concerns and technological shifts redefined the industry. The 1970s oil crises highlighted dependence on fossil fuels, prompting efficiency standards and the revival of electric vehicles; by the 1990s, sport utility vehicles (SUVs) and minivans dominated markets for their versatility. Japan overtook as the world's top auto producer by 1980, emphasizing quality and fuel efficiency. The 21st century brought electrification and autonomy, with Tesla surpassing traditional automakers in market value by 2020 through production of over 500,000 electric vehicles annually, incorporating advanced batteries and Level 2 autonomous driving features. These developments continue to address sustainability, with fully electric and hybrid models reducing emissions while integrating computer-aided design and global supply chains.
